result.summary: After a defeat the Spartans consult Delphi and try deception, first with fake deserters and then with clay tripods set up at Ithome. Aristodemus rejects the deserters and receives obscure oracles, while Lyciscus is cleared of treason by the priestess of Hera.

scenes.title: Sparta seeks cunning against Ithome
scenes.summary: The Spartans consult Delphi, are told to use cunning, send fake deserters to Ithome and try to win over the Messenians' allies. Aristodemus sees through the deserters and the Arcadians refuse.
scenes.stakes: Sparta risks losing the war; the Messenians risk being deceived.

scenes.title: Aristodemus consults Delphi
scenes.summary: Aristodemus sends to Delphi and gets an obscure oracle about ambush and things changing their nature.
scenes.stakes: The Messenians risk falling to Spartan wiles they cannot foresee.

scenes.title: The case of Lyciscus
scenes.summary: Lyciscus is captured by Arcadian cavalry and brought to Ithome, accused of treason. The priestess of Hera confesses the child was hers, clearing him.
scenes.stakes: Lyciscus risks punishment as a traitor; the priestess loses her priesthood.

scenes.title: The tripods and the trick
scenes.summary: In the twentieth year the Messenians are told to set up 100 tripods first. Œbalus tricks them with clay tripods, and Aristodemus sets up wooden ones. Ophioneus regains his sight.
scenes.stakes: Whoever fails to set the tripods first loses the land and victory.

alias_notes.explanation: Epithet of Apollo, the god who speaks through the Pythian Priestess.

notable_quotes.reason: Aristodemus's sharp reply to the fake deserters.
Oracle's grim saying that ruin comes to peoples in turn.

analysis.text: Cunning and deceit dominate the war, and oracles are ambiguous, rewarding the side that reads them cleverly.
The chapter reflects the Spartan conquest of Messenia and the central role of Delphi in Greek decisions.

fun_facts.text: Pausanias drew his account of the Messenian wars largely from the poet Rhianus and the historian Myron of Priene.

language_notes.text: The oracle says the land was won by cunning, so cunning will take it back; the Spartans read this as permission for trickery.
Refers to Odysseus' trick of entering Troy (Ilium) disguised as a beggar, or to the Wooden Horse; the text names the Greek form, though this translation otherwise varies.
Public condemnation made the pretended desertion look genuine to the Messenians.
Ares stands for war; 'garlands of their dances' means festive wreaths, implying joy turned to mourning. The 'two hidden things' are deliberately unclear.
'Things that change their nature' is a riddle; the god's later fulfilment is meant to explain it.
"Resident alien" translates metoikos, a foreigner living in a city with limited rights and no citizenship.
"Palm off as her own" means to pass the child off as the wife's own by deception.
"Guile moves you on, and behind is vengeance" means deceit drives the Messenians forward while retribution follows close after.
"Ruin takes people by turns" means disaster comes to each side in succession; fortune alternates.
"Clay roughly": the tripods were crudely molded of unfired or cheap clay, enough to pass as offerings at night.
"Conjuncture" means the combination of circumstances, the critical state of affairs.

context_notes.text: Delphi's oracle of Apollo was consulted by Greek states before major decisions; the Pythian Priestess spoke in his name.
Ephors were Spartan magistrates elected annually who, with the two kings, directed state policy.
Arcadia lay between Sparta and Messenia and was a natural ally of the Messenians; Argos was another enemy of Sparta.
Hera was a major goddess, patron of marriage; her priestess held a prestigious hereditary-style office at Messene.
The Pythian Priestess was the Pythia, the woman who delivered Apollo's oracles at Delphi.
A tripod was a three-legged bronze cauldron, a common votive offering to gods. Ithome was the Messenians' mountain stronghold.
Œbalus is a Spartan; Sparta (Lacedæmon) was the Messenians' enemy in this war.

literary_notes.text: Aristodemus' neat contrast of recent injuries and ancient craft shows his shrewdness and Spartan reputation for deceit.
Ares stands for war and death, and dance garlands for peaceful joy, so the oracle speaks in grim symbolic images.
The narrator signals that the riddle will be explained later, building suspense.
The oracle hints that deceit and punishment will come, anticipating the clay-tripod trick and its consequences.
The unremarkable Œbalus solves the problem that stumped the whole Spartan assembly.
Aristodemus is shown as a steady leader who consoles his people and carries on despite the setback.
